title: Laboratory: run the smoothing layer yourself

what.formal: This laboratory evaluates one application of the propagation operator from Equation (1) — $X \leftarrow D_v^{-1/2} H D_e^{-1} H^{\mathsf T} D_v^{-1/2} X$ — on a four-vertex hypergraph whose hyperedges you control. The weight matrix $W$ and the parameter matrix $\Theta$ are set to the identity and the nonlinearity $\sigma$ is omitted, so that the arithmetic of the propagation is visible without a learned transform obscuring it.
what.plain: Slide the four values, press the button, and watch one layer of neighbourhood averaging happen — including what it does to the spread of the values.

what.md: **What to look for while you play.** Three things, in this order. First, watch a single vertex's value after one step and check it against the walkthrough you read in Equation (1)'s card. Second, watch the **range** — the gap between the largest and smallest value — because that is the quantity that measures how much the layer has smoothed. Third, press the button repeatedly and watch the range shrink towards zero: that is over-smoothing, and you are causing it one application at a time.

**Two deliberate omissions, so you do not misread the numbers.** $W = I$ means every hyperedge is weighted equally — in a trained model these weights are learnable. $\Theta = I$ and $\sigma$ omitted means no learned mixing happens between feature channels; with the real $\Theta$ the output is a learned linear combination, and with the sigmoid applied to values like these every entry would saturate to nearly $1$, erasing the differences you are about to watch.

Hypergraph smoothing sandbox — Equation (1)
Vertices v1–v4 with hyperedges e1={1,2}, e2={2,3}, e3={2,4} — a star with v2 at its centre. Optionally add e4={1,2,3}, which makes vertex 2 a hub in a group of three.

example.md: **Task 1 — reproduce the card's walkthrough.** Leave all four sliders at their defaults and the extra hyperedge off, then press *Apply one layer* once.

items.md: Read the vertex degrees shown under the sliders: they should be (1, 3, 1, 1), because vertex 2 belongs to all three hyperedges and the others to one each.
items.why: If the degrees do not match, something has been changed — check the checkbox first. Getting the degrees right before stepping is what makes the next number interpretable.

items.md: Read the four values after the step. They should be close to $10.774$, $33.094$, $20.774$, $25.774$ — matching the walkthrough in Equation (1)'s card to three decimals.
items.why: This is the check that the arithmetic in the card was not a special case. If your numbers match, the card's five moves — damp, collect, average, distribute, damp — are the actual computation.

items.md: Read the range. It should have fallen from $30$ to about $22.3$.
items.why: **This is the number to remember.** One layer contracts the spread by roughly a quarter. That single ratio is the whole of over-smoothing: apply the layer $k$ times and the range is roughly $30 \times r^k$ for some $r < 1$.

example.md: **Task 2 — cause over-smoothing.** Press *Apply one layer* five more times, watching the range after each press.

items.md: Record the range after steps 2, 3 and 4, and compute the ratio between consecutive ranges.
items.why: The ratio should be roughly constant, which is what makes the contraction geometric rather than accidental. A constant ratio is the signature of a linear operator being raised to a power.

items.md: Keep pressing until the range is below about 1, then stop and look at the four values.
items.why: They will all be close to the graph's weighted average. **The information has not been destroyed by an error — it has been averaged away by exactly the operation the method is built on.**

items.md: Press *Reset* and try again with the slider values $10, 20, 30, 40$ replaced by $40, 30, 20, 10$ — the same multiset in a different arrangement. Compare eight steps of each.
items.why: Both converge to the same constant, because the limit depends on the *weights* each vertex carries in the stationary distribution, not on the initial arrangement. Whenever a process forgets its input, the input cannot have been what the process was for.

example.md: **Task 3 — give the hub a group to belong to.** Tick *add hyperedge e4 = {1,2,3}* and press *Apply one layer* from the defaults.

items.md: Check what changed before pressing: vertex degrees are now (2, 4, 2, 1) and hyperedge degrees are (2, 2, 2, 3).
items.why: Adding one relation changed three vertices' degrees and added a relation of size three. Everything downstream of the incidence matrix is now different — which is the point of the exercise.

items.md: Press once and compare the output with the three-hyperedge case.
items.why: The values differ in every coordinate. **A single hyperedge changed the entire layer's output**, which is what makes the construction of hyperedges — the $k$ of Chapter 2's discussion — a modelling decision rather than a preprocessing detail.

quiz.q: With the default sliders and no extra hyperedge, which vertex is damped by $D_v^{-1/2}$ and by how much?

opts.md: All four equally, since the damping is applied to the whole matrix
opts.expl: The matrix $D_v^{-1/2}$ is diagonal, so it multiplies each row by that row's own factor. Entries with the same degree get the same factor; entries with different degrees do not.

opts.md: Vertex 2 only, by a factor of $1/\sqrt{3}$, because its degree is 3 while the others have degree 1
opts.expl: Correct. Vertices 1, 3 and 4 have degree 1, so their factor is $1/\sqrt{1} = 1$ — unchanged. Vertex 2's value is divided by $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, which is why 20 becomes 11.547 in the walkthrough.

opts.md: Vertex 4, because it is the last in the path
opts.expl: Position in the path is irrelevant; only the degree enters the damping. Vertex 4 has degree 1, so it is not damped at all.

quiz.q: With e4 added, how many memberships does the hypergraph contain in total?
quiz.hint: Add up the sizes of the four hyperedges.
quiz.sol: The hyperedges are $\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{3,4\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$, of sizes 2, 2, 2 and 3, so the total is $2+2+2+3 = 9$. Equivalently, sum the vertex degrees: $2+4+2+1 = 9$. The two routes agreeing is the handshake identity from the graph-theory section, now on a live object.

quiz.q: After enough presses of *Apply one layer*, what happens to four vertices that started with very different values?

opts.md: They keep their differences but shift downward
opts.expl: A constant offset would be a translation, which this operator does not perform. It averages, and averaging compresses differences.

opts.md: They converge to a common value and the range goes to zero
opts.expl: Correct. Each application replaces every value with a blend of related values, and repeated blending has a unique fixed point: the constant signal. This is over-smoothing, produced by the method's own layer rather than by any bug in it — and it is why the paper's introduction names it as the first failure of the prior paradigm.

Oscillation requires the operator to have complex eigenvalues of modulus one. This one is symmetric and positive semi-definite with eigenvalues in $[0, 1]$, so repeated application converges rather than oscillating.
